sections.title: TRANSITION WEEK
sections.description:
Hi Team,

We’re wrapping up our current training block this week.

Week 4/4 will be what I call a transition week.

What does that mean? After three weeks of rigid, structured progressions, we're going to change things up slightly. We do so in order to balance the rigidity and flexibility that make up a great training program for CrossFit. 
Too much structure and set systems has its limitations, just as too much variance and chaos does.
For us, based on the last 11 years of programming/training/coaching, we've found a 3-week "on" / 1-week "off" routine to be the most effective way to balance out the above.

There will be less training overall this week to allow for better quality and better recovery, so that you are ready for a new training week starting next Monday. (One session a day)
 
Intensity is self-regulated. If you feel great, push. If you don’t, dial it back.
_______________________
Monday 2nd of November we start fresh and continue our progressive overload with the Heavy/Light design. I can’t wait to show you what’s coming.
– André Houdet
nst

sections.title: CURRENT TRAINING BLOCK W4/4
sections.description:
Welcome to week 4 of our new training block Team,
If you just joined the team, make sure to read below:

I encourage you to watch the block explanation video below that will give you a deep insight into how the program is structured from a macro to micro level (Global-->Weekly-->Daily overview). 
Video link (block explanation): https://youtu.be/0X1mtEPrfug

If you do not have the time to watch the block explanation video, you can as always read the detailed notes attached in each section of the program to understand the intent behind everything. Due to FITr's layout, we have added the text as attachments to have less text in each box.

Our goal with this training program is to have you feel:
a. Constant progress through consistent good training weeks.
b. Feeling good (injury free)
c. Motivated and driven as you see and understand the intention of how the program is structured.

Our training principles to have success with the program:
#1 If you want to be good at something, you must above all else,
be consistent.
#2 Minimum Effective dose: This is a principle that we use to underline the concept of more frequent good training sessions leads to better results long term. Often if we train too hard we also need a longer recovery time before we can train hard again. Rather keep 5% in the tank instead of overreaching. Typically, people who do not take the needed recovery time from the sessions where they did more than they should end up injured/hits a plateau. We do not need to go to the maximum every time to create adaptation. 
#3 Self-regulation: Listen to your body and adjust the intensity based on how you feel.
#4 Consistently good rather than occasionally great: Many good sessions are always better than a few great. 
#5 The devil is in the detail: Be deliberate and pay attention to set up/reps/tempo/intensity described in the program. 
#6 Stay in your lane: Don’t get caught up in anybody else’s game, you focus on you and your progress.
#7 Technique > Load
#8 Quality > Quantity
#9 Principles > Methods
--------------------------------------
Have a great training block team,
/𝙰𝚗𝚍𝚛𝚎 𝙷𝚘𝚞𝚍𝚎𝚝
𝙳𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚝𝚘𝚛 𝚘𝚏 𝚃𝚛𝚊𝚒𝚗𝚒𝚗𝚐.
𝚗𝚜𝚝.

sections.title: UNDERSTANDING THE DESIGNS
sections.description:
NST Block & Mesocycle Designs

In our last training blocks, we introduced a new program structure that we call the Upper/Lower design

We didn't change what we train. We changed how we organize it.

As I explained across the last few training block videos, each design has its own strengths and weaknesses. To get the best of both worlds, we are alternating between the Upper/Lower- and the Heavy/Light design.

By alternating between the two, we expose you to different ways of distributing training stress while continuing to train the same physical qualities.

This gives us access to the strengths of both systems, allows us to manage training stress in different ways, and helps us continue developing the most well-rounded fitness.

For this training block, after the last 4 weeks of the Heavy/Light design we're going to use the Upper/Lower design.

Below, I've elaborated on the what, why, and how behind both designs so that you can understand the reasoning behind each one and how they affect your training.

1. Our Heavy/Light Design
Our Heavy/Light design organizes the week primarily around the type of stress we're applying.

We alternate between:
Heavy days:
-Absolute Strength
-Absolute Speed
-Weightlifting / Strength-speed / Power
-Strength-endurance / Hypertrophy
-Strength Accessory

and

Light days:
-Gymnastics (Press, Pull, Compress)
-Conditioning (Low-intensity work / Threshold work / VO₂ max)

The idea isn't that "Heavy" means hard and "Light" means easy.
Rather, we're changing how the body is being stressed.
Heavy days generally have greater mechanical and neural demands, while our Light days generally involve less mechanical strain and allow us to place more emphasis on metabolic and gymnastics work.
This gives each day a very clear purpose.
When you come into a Heavy day, you know we're there to develop strength and power.
When you come into a Light day, you know we're there to develop your engine and gymnastics capacity.
That clarity is one of the major strengths of this system.
It also makes it very easy for us to introduce specific biases when we want to emphasize a particular quality. That's why we offer a STR/WL bias and GYM/COND. bias for Power Hour and Compete when using this design.

2. Why add another design structure if this one works?
Because there isn't one perfect structure that works.
Every structure has strengths and limitations.
When you use the same structure for a long period of time, you become very efficient at handling the way that particular structure distributes stress.
That's not necessarily a bad thing. In fact, adaptation is exactly what we're looking for.
But we can continue progressing by changing how we organize the training stimulus without having to completely change what we're training.
That's what we're doing here.
We're not throwing away our Heavy/Light (as you can see, we are back to it this block)
We've just added another tool (Upper/Lower design).

3. Our Upper/Lower Design
The Upper/Lower design organizes the week differently.
Instead of asking:
"What type of stress are we applying today?"
we primarily ask:
"Where are we applying the stress today?"
We alternate between:
Upper-body biased days and Lower-body biased days.
We're still training the same physical qualities we did before. We're simply distributing the stress differently.

4. What Are We Trying to Achieve With Upper/Lower when we use it?
The biggest difference is how we distribute muscular stress and training volume across the week.
In Heavy/Light, we often touch many movement patterns and muscle groups across consecutive days, even though the overall type of stress changes.
With Upper/Lower, we can concentrate more of the work for a particular region into its designated day and then give that region more time before exposing it to another major stimulus.
This gives us a different way of distributing volume and managing local muscular fatigue.
It also allows us to create more concentrated exposures to particular muscle groups and movement patterns.
Instead of having every day contain a little bit of everything, we can create days with a clearer anatomical emphasis.

5. The Trade-Off
There is always a trade-off.
The Heavy/Light design gives us a very clear separation between different types of stress.
It is excellent for protecting the quality of strength and weightlifting work and for creating clear training priorities.
The Upper/Lower design gives us a different advantage: it allows us to distribute muscular volume and local fatigue differently while giving us more flexibility in how we combine training qualities within a session.
So we're exchanging some of the strengths of Heavy/Light for some of the strengths of Upper/Lower.
That's intentional.

6. Why Are We Alternating Them?
Going forward, we will be alternating between the two designs from block to block.
Each block is 4 weeks.
So you will have:
Block 1: Heavy/Light
Block 2: Upper/Lower (3 Upper, 2 Lower)
Block 3: Heavy/Light 
Block 4: Upper/Lower (2 Upper, 3 Lower) (Current block)
And so on.
The goal isn't to constantly change things for the sake of change.
The goal is to use each system where it provides the most value.
By alternating between the two, we expose you to different ways of distributing training stress while continuing to train the same underlying physical qualities.
This gives us access to the strengths of both systems, allows us to manage fatigue in different ways, and gives us more flexibility in how we develop well-rounded fitness over time.

7. The Big Picture
So, if you remember only one thing from this explanation, remember this:
We're not changing what we train. We're changing how we organize it.
Heavy/Light organizes training primarily around the type of stress.
Upper/Lower organizes training primarily around where that stress is applied.
Both systems have strengths.
Both systems have limitations.
And rather than choosing one and sticking with it forever, we're going to use both.
Because our goal isn't simply to make you good at one training structure.
Our goal is to build the most well-rounded, capable, and sustainable athlete possible.
//André
nst

sections.title: STRENGTH-SPEED (Snatch)
sections.description:
Strength-Speed / "Power" / Weightlifting, Squat Snatch (Transition week)

Transition week: Our transition week is all about waving progressive overload to ensure long-term, sustainable progress. This week gives you a break from the last 3 weeks of progression and an opportunity to change the training stimulus, not just through lighter loads, but also through different exercise variations and set-ups.
This week, we'll be using single arm variations in the Squat Snatch to continue working on snatch mechanics while keeping overall strain low through lighter loads and reduced volume. It's also a great way to challenge you mobility-wise and correct potential imbalances.
----------------------------------
a. Build-up to a heavy 5/5 Single DB Squat Snatch from the floor.

b. 3 sets,
30 sec AMRAP Single DB Squat Snatch (right arm)
- rest 60 sec-
30 sec AMRAP Single DB Squat Snatch (left arm)
- rest 60 sec-

(Suggested) Load: Use around 75–85% of the heaviest set of 5 from part a. 
Example: if you built up to 40kg in the first part, aim for a DB between 30 and 34kg.

I don't have access to heavy DB's, what should I do?
a. Build up to a technical set of 5 touch-and-go Barbell Squat Snatches.
b. Perform 3 sets of 30-second AMRAP touch-and-go Squat Snatches at 75–85% of the heavy 5 from part "a" with 90 sec rest between.

Progression:
W1: 6 sets of 3 Hang Squat Snatches (from the blocks). 
W2: 6 sets of 3 Low Hang Squat Snatches (from the blocks), aim to progress loads. 
W3: 6 sets of 3 (1.1.1) Squat Snatches (from the floor), aim to progress loads. 
W4: Transition week (Current) (DB focused work)
----------------------------------
Read more about how weightlifting is developed in our program in attached document.

sections.title: ABSOLUTE STRENGTH (Front Squat)
sections.description:
Strength, Anterior Lower-body (Front Squat) (Transition week)

Transition week: Our transition week is all about waving progressive overload to ensure long-term, sustainable progress. This week gives you a break from the last 3 weeks of progression and an opportunity to change the training stimulus, not just through lighter loads, but also through different exercise variations and set-ups.

During this transition week, we will focus on a static-dynamic approach, combining an isometric variation with a dynamic one. Isometrics are less stressful on the joints, tendons, and muscles while allowing you to produce high levels of force. Dynamic variations allow for greater speed development. Together, both qualities develop power (force × speed).
----------------------------------
a. 4 sets, Going every 3rd minute:
5-10 sec Overcoming isometrics Front squat
-Directly into-
A "tough" set of double DB's Thrusters 

A tough set: Stop 2-4 reps before failure. Cap at 15 reps.

What range should I use for the isometrics?
Work around your sticking point (usually at parallel or slightly above)

Load: 
[Double DB Thrusters]
(Elite) ♂ 2x32.5kg/70lbs ⎸♀ 2x22.5kg/50lbs
(Rx) ♂ 2x22.5kg/50lbs ⎸♀ 2x15kg/35lbs
(Intermediate) ♂ 2x17.5kg/40lbs ⎸♀ 2x12.5/30lbs

Progression:
W1: 3 sets of 3 Front Squats (31X1) + 3 sets of 3 Front Squats (no tempo restrictions). 
W2: Same volume and format, aim to progress loads.
W3: Same volume and format, aim to progress loads. 
W4: Transition week. (Current) (Iso work + DB work)
----------------------------------
Read more about how strength is developed in our program in attached document.

sections.title: (TEAM VERSION) CONDITIONING
sections.description:
Note: One of the reasons most of us fall in love with CrossFit is the community aspect.
It’s being surrounded by others whom are like minded in an environment that brings out the best in us.
Pushing hard in training with a group can for some feel more enjoyable and can often give that extra kick needed to perform better.
The "Team Edition" add-ons to the program is for those who wishes to do team competitions now and in the future.
This will give those of you who might consider going team a structured session that will be based around synchro coordination, team workouts, relays & worm specific training. All elements that are key in creating a successful team.

It can be hard to coordinate training with 3 others and the program is therefore build in a way that the team session fits in with the rest of the weekly program, so that we make sure you hit everything you need to weekly.

This piece is to be done instead of the original engine piece.
_________________________________________
Conditioning

a. Team of 4
 20 min EMOM 
Min 1: 4 Worm Clean C&J + 35 Double Unders (each)
Min 2: 12 Burpees over the worm
Min 3: Max calories Ski Erg (each, at the same time)
Min 4: Rest

sections.title: STRENGTH ENDURANCE (Unilateral)
sections.description:
Strength Endurance, Lower-body (Unilateral)

a. 6 sets, 1 minute AMRAP / 1 minute Rest (Alternate arms each set)
5 Double DB Devil Presses + 5 Double DB Hang Snatches + max distance Double DB OH Lunges

Load:
(Elite) ♂ 2x22.5kg/50lbs ⎸ ♀ 2x15kg/35lbs
(Rx) ♂ 2x17.5kg/40lbs ⎸ ♀ 2x12.5kg/30lbs
(Intermediate) ♂ 2x15kg/35lbs ⎸ ♀ 2x10kg/20lbs

Flow explained: This week, we are increasing difficulty by keeping interference while working with a double arm variation again. 
During each 1 minute AMRAP, work continuously with two DB's without putting them down: 5 Double DB Devil Press + 5 Double DB Snatch + max distance Double DB OH Walking Lunges.
After your 1:00 rest, start again.

Tempo: Quality and control is key.

sections.title: TRANSITION WEEK
sections.description:
Hi Team,

We’re wrapping up our current training block this week.

Week 4/4 will be what I call a transition week.

What does that mean? After three weeks of rigid, structured progressions, we're going to change things up slightly. We do so in order to balance the rigidity and flexibility that make up a great training program for CrossFit. 
Too much structure and set systems has its limitations, just as too much variance and chaos does.
For us, based on the last 11 years of programming/training/coaching, we've found a 3-week "on" / 1-week "off" routine to be the most effective way to balance out the above.

There will be less training overall this week to allow for better quality and better recovery, so that you are ready for a new training week starting next Monday. (One session a day)
 
Intensity is self-regulated. If you feel great, push. If you don’t, dial it back.
_______________________
Monday 2nd of November we start fresh and continue our progressive overload with the Heavy/Light design. I can’t wait to show you what’s coming.
– André Houdet

sections.title: OPTION 1: FULL REST / BODYWORK
sections.description:
Recovery is what allows athletes to train at a consistently high level and perform to the best of their abilities.

The hours outside of training play a major role in how effectively you recover from training stressors.

To get the most out of an athlete, it’s essential to find the right balance between training overload and sufficient recovery. Short periods of increased training stress can temporarily reduce performance and increase fatigue, but when paired with adequate recovery, this can lead to positive adaptation and improved performance. In sport science, this is referred to as Functional Overreaching (FOR). However, when recovery is insufficient and fatigue continues to accumulate without adequate adaptation, athletes may enter a state of Non-Functional Overreaching (NFOR), where performance begins to stagnate or decline.

We aim to create the right balance by periodizing the program appropriately while also encouraging athletes to self-regulate when needed.

Here are some signs that recovery may be compromised:

-Inability to sustain efforts during high-intensity exercise
-Increased fatigue during and after training
-Low mood or reduced motivation
-Sleep disturbances
-Persistent soreness or slower recovery between sessions

It’s important to understand that stressors outside of training are often the biggest obstacle to recovery. Start by analyzing and optimizing the 18–22 hours of the day spent away from training.

Below are several recovery methods that may help support overall recovery and performance:

#1 Additional Sleep
Sleep remains the most effective and important recovery tool available to athletes.

#2 Methods That May Support Blood Flow and Reduce Muscle Soreness
The following methods may help increase circulation, promote relaxation, and improve perceived recovery:
-Professional bodywork such as physiotherapy or massage
-Recovery boots/compression therapy
-Self-myofascial release (foam rolling, lacrosse balls, etc.)
-Muscle stimulation devices such as Compex

#3 Additional Recovery Strategies
These are methods I’ve personally experimented with and occasionally use when feeling the need for some extra recovery support:
-Epsom salt baths
-Meditation — recovery is not only physical, but also psychological
-Barefoot walks on grass/"earthing" — while scientific evidence is limited, some athletes find it relaxing and helpful for stress reduction
-Increased sunlight exposure to support circadian rhythm, mood, and sleep quality
-Light water movement sessions — the hydrostatic pressure and low-impact nature of water can help promote movement and recovery without adding significant stress to the body

sections.title: STRENGTH-SPEED (Jerk)
sections.description:
Strength-Speed / "Power" / Weightlifting, Jerk (any)(Transition week)

Transition week: Our transition week is all about waving progressive overload to ensure long-term, sustainable progress. This week gives you a break from the last 3 weeks of progression and an opportunity to change the training stimulus, not just through lighter loads, but also through different exercise variations and set-ups.
This week, we'll be using single arm variations in the Jerk to continue working on jerk mechanics while keeping overall strain low through lighter loads and reduced volume. It's also a great way to challenge you mobility-wise and correct potential imbalances.
----------------------------------
a. Build-up to a heavy 5/5 Single DB Jerk (any) from the floor.

b. 3 sets,
30 sec AMRAP Single DB Jerk (any) (right arm)
- rest 60 sec-
30 sec AMRAP Single DB Jerk (any) (left arm)
- rest 60 sec-

(Suggested) Load: Use around 75–85% of the heaviest set of 5 from part a. 
Example: if you built up to 40kg in the first part, aim for a DB between 30 and 34kg — so either 30kg or 32.5kg.

I don't have access to heavy DB's, what should I do?
a. Build up to a technical set of 5 touch-and-go barbell Push Press.
b. Perform 3 sets of 30-second AMRAP touch-and-go Push Press at 75–85% of the heavy 5 from part "a" with 90 sec rest between.

Progression:
W1: 6 sets of 3 Jerk (any) (2 pauses). 
W2: 6 sets of 3 Jerk (any) (1 pause), aim to progress loads. 
W3: 6 sets of 3 Jerk (any) (no pause), aim to progress loads. 
W4: Transition week. (Current)

Transition week: Our transition week is all about waving progressive overload to ensure long-term, sustainable progress. This week gives you a break from the last 3 weeks of progression and an opportunity to change the training stimulus, not just through lighter loads, but also through different exercise variations and set-ups.

During this transition week, we will focus on a static-dynamic approach, combining an isometric variation with a dynamic one. Isometrics are less stressful on the joints, tendons, and muscles while allowing you to produce high levels of force. Dynamic variations allow for greater speed development. Together, both qualities develop power (force × speed).

It’s being surrounded by others whom are like minded in an environment that brings out the best in us.
Pushing hard in training with a group can for some feel more enjoyable and can often give that extra kick needed to perform better.
The "Team Edition" add-ons to the program is for those who wishes to do team competitions now and in the future.
This will give those of you who might consider going team a structured session that will be based around synchro coordination, team workouts, relays & worm specific training. All elements that are key in creating a successful team.

It can be hard to coordinate training with 3 others and the program is therefore build in a way that the team session fits in with the rest of the weekly program, so that we make sure you hit everything you need to weekly.

This piece is to be done instead of the original engine piece.
_________________________________________
Conditioning

a. Team of 4
5 sets, "You Go, We Go" (One M/F pair is working, the other pair is resting)
10/8 calories Echo Bike (each, at the same time)
5 Sync. Ring MU
10/8 calories Echo Bike (each, at the same time)
6 Sync. Conga Line Power Clean (185/125lbs ⎸ 84/56kg)

sections.title: FULL REST DAY
sections.description:
Goals for today:

a. Meal prep and Snack prep to make the coming week easier. You don't have to prep for the whole week, but having prepped a few meals and making sure you have snacks/fruits to help you stay fueled can be the difference maker in having a good or bad training week.

b. Take a break = Relax / don't talk about CrossFit / Get out of the gym / spend time with family and friends.

c. Take care of practical things that you don't want to and don't have time to deal with during the week = Washing clothes, paying bills, cleaning the car etc.

d. Give yourself a tap on the shoulder for what you have done this week training wise. Regardless of having done great or not, you have done work, and every bit counts in the process of making you fitter than you were.
